blocks.text: A **percentage** expresses a number as a fraction of 100. It is the basis of profit-loss, interest, data interpretation and much of commercial arithmetic — so quick percentage-fraction conversions save time.

items: A rise of x% then a fall of x% gives a **net loss of x²/100 %**.
Memorise **fraction-to-percentage** conversions for speed.
**x% = x/100**; a is what % of b → (a/b)×100; **% change = (change/original)×100**.
**Increase then decrease by same %**: net = −(x²/100)% (always a loss); successive changes a%,b% → **a+b+(ab/100)%**.
**Population/appreciation**: A = P(1 ± r/100)ⁿ.

blocks.text: Solved: 20% of 350 = **70**. || A number increased 20% then decreased 20% → net −4% (=−20²/100). || If price rises 25%, reduce consumption by 25/125×100 = **20%** to keep expenditure same.

prelimsPointers: Successive changes a% then b% → net = **a + b + ab/100** (signs matter).
Increase then decrease by same x% → **net loss = x²/100 %**.
If A is x% more than B, B is **less than A by x/(100+x)×100 %**.
Population/CI-type growth over n years uses **(1 ± r/100)ⁿ**.
Successive % changes a,b → **a+b+ab/100**; equal +x% then −x% → net **−x²/100**.
If price ↑ by x%, cut consumption by **x/(100+x)×100%** to hold spend constant.

glossary.definition: A ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
Two or more percentage changes applied one after another, combined by a+b+ab/100.

blocks.text: **Interest** is the cost of borrowing. **Simple interest (SI)** is computed only on the principal, while **compound interest (CI)** is computed on principal plus accumulated interest — hence CI grows faster.

items: For 2 years, **CI − SI = P·(R/100)²** — a fast formula.
CI ≥ SI always (equal only for 1 year, annual compounding).

sections.heading: 🔢 Formulae & solved examples: simple & compound interest

items: **Simple Interest (SI)** = **P·R·T/100**; Amount = P+SI.
**Compound Interest (CI)**: Amount = **P(1+R/100)ⁿ**; CI = Amount − P.
**Half-yearly** compounding: rate R/2, time 2n; **doubling** — SI doubles in 100/R years; CI ~ '**rule of 72**' (years to double ≈ 72/R).
**Effective rate** > nominal when compounded more often.

prelimsPointers: CI and SI are **equal for the first year** (annual compounding).

glossary.definition: Interest calculated only on the original principal (SI = PRT/100).
Interest calculated on principal plus previously accrued interest.

blocks.text: **Profit and loss** problems compare **cost price (CP)** and **selling price (SP)**. Profit or loss is always calculated **as a percentage of the cost price** (unless stated otherwise), and discounts apply to the **marked price**.

items: Profit/loss % is **always on the cost price** unless stated.
Selling two items at the same price with equal +x% and −x% → **net loss x²/100 %**.
**Profit = SP − CP**; **Loss = CP − SP**; **Profit% = (Profit/CP)×100** (always on CP).
**Discount** is on **Marked Price (MP)**: SP = MP(1 − d/100); **markup** on CP.
**Dishonest dealer / false weight**: gain% = (error / (true value − error))×100.
Two articles sold at same SP, one at +x% & other at −x% → **net loss = x²/100 %**.

prelimsPointers: Profit/loss is reckoned on **CP** unless otherwise stated.
**Discount is on the Marked Price**, not the cost price.
Two articles at same SP, one +x% one −x% → **net loss = x²/100 %**.
Successive discounts a% and b% → net = **a + b − ab/100**.
Dishonest dealer using false weight: gain% = (error/(true−error))×100.
**Profit% always on CP**; discount always on **Marked Price**.
Two items at same SP, +x% & −x% → **net loss x²/100%**.

glossary.definition: The price at which an article is bought.
The listed price before discount, on which discount is calculated.

blocks.text: **Time-and-work** problems relate the **rate of work** to the time taken. If a person completes a job in n days, their one-day work is **1/n**; combined rates add up.

rows: If A does a job in n days, rate = **1/n**.
Wages split in **ratio of work done** (or efficiency).

items: A in a days, B in b days → together in **ab/(a+b)** days.
**Efficiency ∝ 1/time**; use the LCM (total work) method for multi-worker sums.
If A does a job in **n days**, A's 1-day work = **1/n**; combined rate adds up.
**A & B together** in T = **(a·b)/(a+b)** days (a,b = individual days).
**Work ∝ men × days × hours**: **(M₁D₁H₁)/W₁ = (M₂D₂H₂)/W₂**.
**Efficiency**: more efficient → fewer days (inverse); pipes & cisterns — inlet +, outlet −.
**Wages ∝ work done** (share of the job).

blocks.text: Solved: A in 12 d, B in 6 d → together = 12·6/(12+6) = **4 days**. || A pipe fills in 4 h, a leak empties in 6 h → net fill = 1/4−1/6 = 1/12 → **12 hours**. || 6 men, 8 h, 10 d do a job → 4 men need (6·8·10)/(4·8) = **15 days**.

prelimsPointers: One-day work of A (does job in n days) = **1/n**.
A & B together finish in **ab/(a+b)** days.
**LCM method**: take total work = LCM of days, find each rate as units/day.
Wages are divided in the **ratio of work done**.
Pipes: inlet **+1/t**, outlet **−1/t**; net rate decides fill/empty time.
Wages split in ratio of **work done (rates)**.

glossary.definition: The fraction of a job completed in unit time (1/n per day if the job takes n days).
Taking total work as the LCM of the given times to simplify time-and-work sums.

blocks.text: **Speed, time and distance** are linked by **Distance = Speed × Time**. Problems cover average speed, relative speed (trains, boats), and unit conversions — a high-frequency CSAT area.

rows: Total distance / total time; for equal distances = **2xy/(x+y)**.

items: **km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18** (and reverse by 18/5).
Average speed for equal distances = **harmonic mean 2xy/(x+y)**, NOT the simple average.

sections.heading: 🔢 Formulae & solved examples: time, speed & distance

items: **Speed = Distance/Time**; **Distance = Speed×Time**; **Time = Distance/Speed**.
**Unit conversion**: km/h → m/s **×5/18**; m/s → km/h **×18/5**.
**Average speed** (equal distances at u & v) = **2uv/(u+v)** (harmonic mean).
**Relative speed**: same direction = (a−b); opposite = (a+b).

**Trains**: crossing a pole = length/speed; crossing a platform = (train+platform)/speed; **boats & streams** — downstream = (b+s), upstream = (b−s); speed in still water = (down+up)/2, stream = (down−up)/2.

blocks.text: Solved: 72 km/h = 72×5/18 = **20 m/s**. || Avg speed 60 & 40 km/h equal distances = 2·60·40/100 = **48 km/h**. || Train 150 m at 20 m/s crosses a 250 m platform in (150+250)/20 = **20 s**. || Boat 10 km/h, stream 2 → downstream **12**, upstream **8**.

prelimsPointers: Average speed (equal distances at x, y) = **2xy/(x+y)**.
**Boats**: downstream = boat + stream; upstream = boat − stream.
Train crossing a pole: distance = **train length**; crossing a platform: **train + platform length**.
Average speed (equal distances) = **2uv/(u+v)** (not the arithmetic mean).

glossary.definition: The speed of one moving object with respect to another (sum if opposite, difference if same direction).
Total distance divided by total time; for equal distances it is the harmonic mean of the speeds.
